newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia curbs poll campaigning to avoid unrest.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia curbs poll campaigning to avoid unrest.

text.p: Indonesia's government, shaken by riots in different parts of the sprawling country, is restricting campaigning for May general elections to offset further violence, political analysts said on Wednesday.
"The moves are basically designed to reduce the possibility of random clashes," a senior diplomatic source said.

An election commission official said poll speeches would be vetted before broadcast. The government has banned campaign advertising, and there are also restrictions on public gatherings and election aids such as posters and brochures.

Diplomatic analysts note the result of the May 29 elections is beyond doubt, with the ruling Golkar the assured victor and the other two parties legally entitled to contest the poll trailing far behind.

In the last elections in 1992, Golkar won 68 percent of the vote, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) 17 percent and the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) -- now riven by internal disputes -- 15 percent.
Political analysts say the most interesting factor in the election will be the percentage received by Golkar, with President Suharto's government pushing hard to raise its share above 70 percent.
But Indonesia, the world's fourth most populous country with 200 million people, has been rocked by a series of riots sparked by seemingly trivial incidents in recent months.
A riot involving thousands of local Dayaks and resettled Maduran islanders in West Kalimantan province on Borneo island at the beginning of January was set off by a fight over a girl.
In West Java, a report of police brutality sparked a riot in the town of Tasikmalaya in which shops, homes and churches were burned down.

A complaint by an ethnic Chinese woman over noise made by youths calling Moslems to their pre-dawn Ramadan breakfast in late January in a small town east of Jakarta led to further wrecking, burning and looting.
Indonesia's armed forces chief General Feisal Tanjung has warned that the military will take "sterner action" to prevent such outbreaks in the future.

Political and social analysts have blamed the eruptions on socio-economic tensions. Government officials speak darkly of a clandestine "third force" linked to a communist conspiracy to destabilise the country.

Some political and diplomatic analysts say change is in the air in Indonesia, with a major question mark hanging over the country's political future once President Suharto -- one of the world's longest-serving leaders -- leaves the scene.

He is widely expected to seek a seventh five-year term of office in a presidential vote due next year. But he is 75 and markets are regularly shaken by persistent rumours about his health. He has yet to designate a successor.
With a rising middle class, there is also some element of frustration with the grip a relatively small group of people -- including members of Suharto's family -- have on the economy.

"There is a general feeling that there ought to be some sort of change. There is the poverty gap. And there is growing frustration at institutional corruption in the police, judiciary and among local officials that can lead to trouble," one political analyst said.
